subject: Biology
title: Ocean Acidification
description: A quick, practical guide to Ocean Acidification.

hook.text: The ocean absorbs about 30% of human CO₂ emissions. But that favor comes with a chemical cost.

buildup.text: CO₂ dissolves in seawater and forms carbonic acid, lowering the ocean's pH.

discovery.text: Acidification dissolves the calcium carbonate shells of oysters, clams, and coral-building organisms.

twist.text: Ocean acidity has increased 30% since the Industrial Revolution—faster than any change in 300 million years.

climax.text: If acidification continues, entire marine food webs built on shell-forming organisms could collapse.

punchline.text: The ocean absorbed our CO₂. Now it's paying the price.

quiz.question: How much has ocean acidity increased since the Industrial Revolution?

details.summary: Ocean acidification occurs when seawater absorbs excess atmospheric CO2, forming carbonic acid that lowers pH. Since industrialization, ocean pH has dropped by 0.1 units, a 30 percent increase in acidity that threatens shell-building organisms from corals to oysters.
details.whyItMatters: Acidification is called climate change's evil twin because it threatens marine food webs independently of warming. Shell-building organisms at the base of many food chains are directly impaired, potentially cascading through entire ocean ecosystems.
takeaways: The ocean has absorbed about 30 percent of human CO2 emissions since industrialization
Lower pH reduces carbonate availability needed for shells and skeletons
Pteropod snails, crucial in polar food webs, show dissolving shells in acidified water

faq.question: Why does absorbing CO2 make the ocean more acidic?
faq.answer: CO2 reacts with seawater to form carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions that lower pH. This also reduces carbonate ion concentration that corals, shellfish, and plankton need to build calcium carbonate shells and skeletons.

faq.question: Which marine organisms are most threatened by acidification?
faq.answer: Organisms that build calcium carbonate structures are most vulnerable, including corals, oysters, mussels, sea urchins, and planktonic pteropods. Pteropods are particularly concerning because they are foundational prey for fish, whales, and seabirds in polar waters.
